doc.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview

title: The tenor craze and Bird's shadow over alto players
summary: In 1946-47 everyone wanted to play tenor; Ware says Bird drove altos away from their horns and some players switched to bass.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Who were some of the other people that

Gene Ammons was around -- he came back; that was his home. And these cats were just starting ... look, everybody had money in those days, '46 and '47, and like I said, every neighborhood had a little club, had 4 pieces, and musicians were coming out of the woodwork; in fact, they were working -- but it all had to do with tenor saxophone -- trumpet players didn't have too much work, you know, but saxophones had it.

Lester Young, the big bands had broke up, you might say; they didn't have too much work, and the leading bars for a combo was a saxophone, and everybody was playing tenors, even -- there were no alto players out there, because Bird seemed to have wiped them off the face of the earth. Really, everybody wanted to play tenor, and some of them were using the technique that Bird was using on the tenors, but that was -- everybody wanted to hear a tenor saxophone -- just everyone.
Do you think people were intimidated by the things that Bird was doing?
Well, I say, like the altos I knew just got out of the service, they switched over to bass. And he

says the reason he switched over to bass, how can he play like that -- and a whole lot of altos had put their horns down because of it. Not really, but they would say, well, what's the use? Everybody expects you to sound like Bird Berg, and if you did, you were copying.
